cards.front: The {{c1::gene pool}} is all the alleles of all the individuals in a population.
cards.quote: The gene pool is all the alleles of all the individuals in a population.

cards.front: An {{c1::allele}} is one version of a gene.
cards.quote: An allele is one version of a gene.

cards.front: Which process is the original source of new alleles in a population?
cards.back: Mutation, a change in an organism's DNA.
cards.quote: It is the original source of new alleles.

cards.front: {{c1::Gene flow}} is the movement of alleles from one population to another, when individuals move and breed or when pollen blows to another field.
cards.quote: Gene flow is the movement of alleles from one population to another, when individuals move and breed or when pollen blows to another field.

cards.front: {{c1::Natural selection}} is the process by which individuals with certain inherited variations survive and reproduce more than others, so those variations become more common in later generations.
cards.quote: Natural selection is the process by which individuals with certain inherited variations survive and reproduce more than others, so those variations become more common in later generations.
cards.section: Explain: what the film left out

cards.front: A {{c1::selective pressure}} is anything in the environment that makes some variants more likely to survive or reproduce than others, such as predators, disease, drought or human hunting.
cards.quote: A selective pressure is anything in the environment that makes some variants more likely to survive or reproduce than others: predators, disease, drought or human hunting.
cards.section: Explain: what the film left out

cards.front: A {{c1::reproductive strategy}} is a species' pattern of how many young it makes and how much it invests in each.
cards.quote: A reproductive strategy is a species' pattern of how many young it makes and how much it invests in each.
cards.section: Explain: what the film left out

cards.front: Sexual reproduction shuffles chromosomes in meiosis. Does it create new alleles? What does it create?
cards.back: No. It makes new combinations of alleles that already exist, so each offspring is a new mix.
cards.why: New alleles come from mutation; sexual reproduction only reshuffles what is already in the gene pool.
cards.quote: This makes new combinations of alleles that already exist, so each offspring is a new mix.

cards.front: What effects can mutations have, and what decides whether one helps?
cards.back: Many have no effect, some harm, and a few help. Whether one helps depends on the environment.
cards.quote: Many mutations have no effect, some harm, and a few help, depending on the environment.

cards.front: Natural selection changes a population only under two conditions. What are they?
cards.back: The variants must be inherited, and the current conditions must make the individuals carrying them leave different numbers of offspring.
cards.quote: It works only when variants are inherited and the current conditions make the individuals that carry them leave different numbers of offspring.

cards.front: In Gorongosa, the share of tuskless females rose after the war. Did individual elephants have to lose their tusks for this to happen? Explain.
cards.back: No. Tuskless females were already in the herd and survived better, so the group percentage changed while no elephant lost her tusks.
cards.quote: No elephant had to lose her tusks for those group percentages to change.

cards.front: Compare the blue crab and the African savanna elephant: young per breeding, care, and survival of each young.
cards.back: Crab: hundreds of thousands to millions of eggs, mother carries them until they hatch, very low survival of each young. Elephant: usually one calf, mother nurses it with births years apart, higher survival of each young.
cards.quote: Neither end of the range is always better; each can leave surviving offspring under some conditions.
cards.section: Explain: what the film left out

cards.front: A female blue crab in the Chesapeake Bay may carry 750,000 to 8 million eggs, yet the crab population does not grow by millions each year. Why not?
cards.back: Populations usually produce more young than can survive. Only a small fraction of the eggs become adults.
cards.quote: Populations usually produce more young than can survive, and individuals whose inherited variations suit the conditions leave more offspring, so those variations become more common.
cards.section: Explain: what the film left out

cards.front: In a population of limited size with no selective pressure, what can chance alone do to a variant over many generations?
cards.back: It can eventually remove that variant entirely, with no consistent direction beforehand.
cards.why: This is genetic drift, a change caused by chance, not by selection.
cards.quote: In a population of limited size, chance alone can eventually remove one variant entirely.
cards.section: Explore: put a population under pressure

cards.front: In Gorongosa National Park, which elephants showed tusklessness?
cards.back: Only females. No tuskless male has been recorded in that park.
cards.quote: In this park tusklessness is seen only in females; no tuskless male has been recorded there.
cards.section: Explain: what the film left out

cards.front: A mutation happens in a skin cell on an elephant's trunk. Could her calf inherit it?
cards.back: No. In most animals, only mutations in the cells that make eggs or sperm pass to offspring, so a skin-cell mutation is not passed on.
cards.quote: In most animals, only mutations in the cells that make eggs or sperm pass to offspring.

cards.front: In Gorongosa, tuskless females rose from 18.5 percent before the war to 50.9 percent among survivors. State the change in percentage points and as a percent change.
cards.back: Percentage points: 50.9 - 18.5 = 32.4. Percent change: 32.4 / 18.5 is about 1.75, a rise of about 175 percent.
cards.quote: As a percent change it is 32.4 ÷ 18.5, a rise of about 175 percent.
cards.section: Elaborate: read the elephant and crab data

cards.front: Wind carries pollen from one field of plants to a second field. The second field's plants lacked one allele that the pollen carries. What does this change in the second field's gene pool?
cards.back: The allele is added to the second field's gene pool. This is gene flow, which can bring in an allele the population did not have.
cards.quote: It can bring in an allele the population did not have.

cards.front: Two model populations start with the same mix of tusked and tuskless animals. One faces strong pressure against tusked animals and the other faces weak pressure. Which changes faster, and why?
cards.back: The strong-pressure population. A strong pressure can change a trait's frequency within a few decades when inherited variation is present, while a weak pressure changes it slowly over many generations.
cards.quote: A strong pressure, like heavy poaching, can change a trait's frequency within a few decades when inherited variation is present.
cards.section: How quickly can a population change?

cards.front: In Gorongosa, 18.5 percent of prewar females had no tusks, 50.9 percent of war survivors had none, and 33 percent of daughters born about 1995 to 2004 had none. Is the daughters' share back at the prewar level?
cards.back: No. At 33 percent it is below the survivors' 50.9 percent but still well above the prewar 18.5 percent, so tuskless females stayed more common.
cards.quote: Before the war, about 1 in 5 of the females researchers sampled had no tusks; among the females that survived the war, about half had none.

cards.front: Researchers estimated that tuskless Gorongosa females survived about five times as well as tusked females. What did they conclude about poaching?
cards.back: Poaching most likely caused strong selection for tusklessness.
cards.quote: Beyond the chance test, the researchers estimated that tuskless females survived about five times as well as tusked females.
cards.section: Explain: what the film left out

cards.front: In a study comparing tuskless females across parks, why should you report the number of animals counted, not only the percentage?
cards.back: A percentage hides the sample size, and one small sample can change by chance. The counts show how much weight each percentage can bear.
cards.quote: Report the number of animals, not only the percentage.

cards.front: In a photo-based count of tusked and tuskless elephants, what could mislead you?
cards.back: Old photos may show some animals more than others, and tuskless elephants may be easier or harder to spot. Recording each known individual once helps.
cards.quote: old photos may show some animals more than others, and tuskless elephants may be easier or harder to spot.

cards.front: A park has strong poaching of tusked females and no tuskless females at all. Can selection alone produce tuskless females there? What would have to happen first?
cards.back: No. A missing variant cannot be selected. A new allele must first arise by mutation, or arrive by gene flow, and then the pressure could favor it.
cards.why: Rests on mutation as the original source of new alleles, gene flow as another source, and selection acting only on variants that exist.
cards.quote: It is the original source of new alleles.

cards.front: A tuskless-female allele arrives in a park by gene flow. Predict its fate under heavy poaching versus no poaching.
cards.back: Under heavy poaching, tuskless females survive and reproduce more, so the allele's share should rise over generations. In the model, with no poaching it changes only by chance, with no consistent direction.
cards.why: Rests on gene flow adding alleles and on selection changing shares only when a pressure makes variants leave different numbers of offspring.
cards.quote: It can bring in an allele the population did not have.

cards.front: Before-and-after data show tuskless females rose in one park. What result in a comparison of parks would support selection by hunting rather than chance?
cards.back: A larger rise in tuskless females in several heavy-poaching parks than in several low-poaching parks, measured over the same years.
cards.why: One park's rise could be chance, so comparing groups with and without the pressure separates the two explanations.
cards.quote: A larger rise in heavy-poaching parks than in low-poaching parks would support selection by hunting.

cards.front: Is a strategy of many young with little care better than few young with much care?
cards.back: Neither is always better. Each can leave surviving offspring under some conditions.
cards.quote: Neither end of the range is always better; each can leave surviving offspring under some conditions.
